processing: Made the way Phoenix dancong usually is: sun-withered, shaken and rested in rounds, then fixed, rolled and dried, with the roast set by the maker.
harvest_season: As with most Phoenix dancong, the spring picking is the main and most prized one.
appearance_dry: Tight, straight strands, yellow-brown and oily, as described for the almond type, and shorter than most dancong.
appearance_liquor: Light yellow and bright, as described for the almond type.
appearance_wet: Leaves with reddened edges, as is usual for well-shaken dancong.
taste_profile: Named for the aroma and taste of the medicinal apricot kernel: an almond character, with the high, lasting scent and strong returning sweetness described for the almond type.

brewing.notes: General dancong approach: very hot water and quick pours. Over-steeping brings bitterness forward.

vintage_note: No selling pattern specific to this line is documented. Phoenix dancong is usually sold by spring harvest of the current year, often after a roast and a rest, and older roasted stock is sold with its year stated.
description:
Lao Xingren Xiang, 'old almond aroma', is a Phoenix Mountain line named for the smell and taste of apricot kernel, the medicinal ingredient. It is listed as a representative of the almond aroma type next to Ju Duo Zai and Wu Ye.

There is little published on how it differs from those two. Processing is presumably the usual dancong sequence of shaking, resting, fixing and drying.

For the almond type in general, expect a clean, high scent with a long sweetness afterwards. Brew it hot and fast like other dancong.

The word 'lao' sells well and can't be checked from the bag, so ask which village and tree a lot comes from. If you enjoy it, Ju Duo Zai is the obvious comparison.
history: Little is documented about when or where this line was selected. It appears in Chinese descriptions of Phoenix lines, explained by its apricot-kernel character and placed in the almond type.
